name: Baltimore Club
about: Baltimore club took shape in the city's Black clubs in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when DJs such as Scottie B, Frank Ski and DJ Technics stitched Chicago house, Miami bass and hip-hop into something faster and blunter. The template has barely moved: around 130 BPM, a stuttering kick pattern, the "Sing Sing" and "Think" breaks looped hard, and a chopped vocal, chant or hook hammered until it becomes a command. Rod Lee, K-Swift, DJ Booman and DJ Class carried it through the 2000s on 12-inches and mixtapes from Unruly and Club Kingz; Blaqstarr and Rye Rye took it into M.I.A.'s orbit; Hollertronix and Spank Rock sold it to indie crowds. It seeded Philly and Jersey club, and TT the Artist and Abdu Ali still work in its grammar.

artists.name: Scottie B
artists.why: Unruly co-founder, the sound's first architect

artists.name: Frank Ski
artists.why: cut the 1993 blueprint with Miss Tony

artists.name: Miss Tony
artists.why: the drag queen voice of the early anthems

artists.name: DJ Technics
artists.why: codified the kick pattern on countless 12-inches

artists.name: Rod Lee
artists.why: Club Kingz boss, the scene's one album artist

artists.name: K-Swift
artists.why: the Club Queen of 92Q radio, died 2008

artists.name: DJ Booman
artists.why: Doo Dew Kidz producer behind the mid-period hits

artists.name: DJ Class
artists.why: took it to national radio in 2009

artists.name: Blaqstarr
artists.why: the eerie minimalist who reached M.I.A.

artists.name: TT the Artist
artists.why: the new generation's standard-bearer and documentarian

artists.name: Abdu Ali
artists.why: bent the club beat toward punk and jazz

albums.title: Vol. 5: The Official
albums.why: The scene's one nationally distributed album: Rod Lee's hoarse, pleading anthems, 'Dance My Pain Away' among them, pressed by Morphius and still the entry point.

albums.title: Never Scared
albums.why: Diplo and Low Budget's mix CD that smuggled Baltimore club breaks into indie parties and set up the mid-2000s boom.

albums.title: Bmore Gutter Music
albums.why: Milkcrate's mixtape primer for outsiders, raw club edits stacked end to end; the record most people outside Baltimore heard first.

albums.title: YoYoYoYoYo
albums.why: Naeem and XXXChange's Big Dada debut, the moment Baltimore club's breaks and filth got an art-rap record and a critical constituency.

albums.title: Supastarr
albums.why: A short EP on M.I.A.'s N.E.E.T. that condenses Blaqstarr's spare, ghostly take on club music, the sound's most distinctive producer at his peak.

albums.title: Twelve Steps
albums.why: The DC DJ's album-length tour of Baltimore club with a crowd of rap and electro guests; polished and fun, a little thin on its own ideas.

albums.title: The Divine
albums.why: A second N.E.E.T. EP that drifts from club tempos toward sung, R&B-shaded hymns; uneven, but the production is as singular as ever.

albums.title: Everything Is Boring and Everyone Is a Fucking Liar
albums.why: The long-delayed follow-up swaps Baltimore breaks for Boys Noize-style electro; a few bangers, but the club roots are mostly gone.

albums.title: Go! Pop! Bang!
albums.why: Years late but still bright: Rye Rye's Interscope debut keeps the Baltimore tempo and chant under pop hooks and M.I.A. and Robyn cameos.

albums.title: Fiyah!!!
albums.why: Baltimore's queer, punk-minded poet sets club rhythms under free-jazz horns and shouted verse, the genre's experimental edge on a full-length.

note: Baltimore club lived on 12-inches, mixtapes and radio rather than albums; this short list is the album-length records that document it.
